doc.title: Derrick Gardner interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 9, 2013

title: Finding your own sound instead of copying
summary: Gardner agrees players today sound alike and says you must imitate first but then move beyond Freddie Hubbard and others to your own voice.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well, you know, and part and parcel with sort of the older generation talking about individuality, a lot of them would also say that nowadays everybody sounds the same, because they’re all using the same books, etcetera. And do you agree with that and if so what do you do about it?

Well you know you have to sound like someone in order to sound like yourself. In the beginning of, in the formative years of your being able to play at an advanced skill level in improvisation, you’d want to sound like somebody else. Like Dizzy Gillespie sounded like Roy Eldridge in those early years. Miles Davis sounded like Dizzy in his early years. And Lee Morgan sounded like Clifford Brown in his early years you know. So when they eventually got tired of playing that way they started going into their own direction. I don’t think that’s happening so much now. You know I hear a lot of the — not just trumpet but even on other instruments — I hear a lot of the younger generation staying in the nest from which they were born you know. A lot of trumpeters are infatuated with Freddie Hubbard, as am I. I will be the first to say that I will have some Freddieisms that will come out in my playing. But I like to think that I have matriculated into something else, you know, and I gauge that by people who say to me, “man I heard this trumpeter on the radio the other day, and I said ‘man, that sounds like Gardner, man, it sounded like Derrick.’” And sure enough, when the guy announced the tune, it was you, man. I said wow. Okay. But that means that I’m suddenly coming into my own sound you know. And he didn’t say it sounded just like Freddie Hubbard, or you sounded just like Clifford Brown you know, which thank you for even associating me to those cats you know. But you have to graduate into your own thing. And I think that that’s what players nowadays have to start pushing for. You can’t just sound like Cannonball forever. You can’t sound like Freddie Hubbard forever. You can’t sound like Paul Chambers or Ron Carter forever. You’ve got to use that as a launching pad into what you’re trying to get into, into your own voice. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -13-
